The failed tests revealed some subtleties that have been addressed.

In Go, if a pointer to a type explicitly implements an interface, then the dereferenced type will not implement the interface. For example, since `*v1.Time` now explicitly implements the `fmt.Stringer` interface after these changes, then `v1.Time` does not implement the`fmt.Stringer` interface. Therefore, this change also includes changes to formatters so that if a pointer type explicitly implements the `fmt.Stringer` interface, then the pointer type is used.

issue_context.title: v1.Time Stringer implementation does not protect against nil-pointer dereference
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The `v1.Time` struct implements the `Stringer` interface because the embedded type (`time.Time`) does. This is fine in production environments, even when the `*v1.Time` pointer is `nil` because of the [catchPanic](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.17.2:src/fmt/print.go;l=538-544) function in the Go standard library. This function will catch the nil-pointer dereference when trying to call the `String` method on the `nil` `*v1.Time` object. The result is `<nil>` is written.

Again, this is all fine when running a production binary, but causes problems when trying to debug. Specifically, when debugging a program from Goland using `dlv`, the nil-pointer dereference is caught by the debugger and causes execution to pause. It also seems that the debugger does not allow the `catchPanic` function to `recover`. I say this because nil-pointer dereference error occurs constantly going forward (possibly related to the re-queuing nature our operator uses).

If the `v1.Time` object had a `String()` method that protected against nil-pointer dereference (like the [IsZero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time.go#L58-L64) method does), then this would not be a problem.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect that the `v1.Time` object had a `String` method that protects against nil-pointer dereference.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Running the following program:
```
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	v1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
)

func main() {
	t := &v1.Time{}
	fmt.Printf("%s\n", t)

	t = (*v1.Time)(nil)
	fmt.Printf("%s\n", t)

	fmt.Println(t.String())
}
```

will have the output:
```
0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC
<nil>
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x8 pc=0x1401f96]

goroutine 1 [running]:
main.main()
        $GOPATH/src/temp/main.go:16 +0xb6
exit status 2
```

### Anything else we need to know?

If the `&` was removed here, then the output would be `{2017-06-04 21:45:56 -0700 PDT}` (with curly braces).

> If the `&` was removed here, then the output would be `{2017-06-04 21:45:56 -0700 PDT}` (with curly braces).

That is so weird.  This is almost like a golang riddle.  I have expanded your example with an OldTime for comparison and I'm still trying to wrap my head around the differences. https://play.golang.org/p/0BtiqauVhtm

I don't really care for an outcome where .String serialization in normal use-cases changes.

> I don't really care for an outcome where .String serialization in normal use-cases changes

Playing further with the playground, it looks like if we had the method receiver be the struct, the change in serialization goes away: https://play.golang.org/p/PTBw2MI1Kwe

So `(t time) String`
That doesn't address the issue though. See my comment here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/105982#discussion_r742890311
